clue.text: News summary not in for a round

indicators.note: not here says the following word is to be dropped from the news summary

parts.note: a bulletin is a short news summary
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone notes that a brief news report has been left out of a quiz round.
explanation.walkthrough: 'round' looks like a quiz round but is the definition, a single shot of ammunition.
explanation.definitionFit: A round of ammunition is a single shot or cartridge for a gun.

clue.text: Chaff not recommended for senior citizens?

explanation.surface: Teasing banter is jokingly labelled as unsuitable for the elderly.
explanation.walkthrough: The second definition is read as BAD IN AGE: something bad for those advanced in years.
explanation.definitionFit: Chaff is light-hearted teasing talk; split into three words the answer says harmful in old age.

clue.text: Tiller girls in the Globe's second row?

definitions.text: Tiller girls in the Globe's second row?

parts.words: Tiller girls in the Globe's second row?
parts.note: Tiller Girls were a famous dance troupe, but here tillers are women who tilled the soil in wartime Britain, and the globe's earth and a row of troops supply the two words

explanation.surface: A chorus line of Tiller Girls stands in the second row at the Globe theatre.
explanation.walkthrough: The Women's Land Army sent women to farm work in both world wars; the Tiller Girls were a British precision dance troupe.
explanation.definitionFit: Wartime Britain's female farm workers formed an organised body, so they were tillers drawn up in ranks like soldiers.

clue.text: Trees, last of the old English line

indicators.note: last of points to the final letter of the word old

parts.note: LMS was the London, Midland and Scottish Railway, an English rail line

explanation.surface: A row of trees is described as the final remnant of an old English line.
explanation.walkthrough: LMS (London, Midland and Scottish) was one of Britain's big four railway companies before nationalisation.
explanation.definitionFit: These are tall deciduous hardwoods once common in English hedgerows.

clue.text: Disappointing scene, perhaps, of misdeeds

parts.note: off can mean poor or disappointing, as in an off day

indicators.note: perhaps signals that the word scene may be rearranged into another possible form

explanation.surface: A disappointing scene showing someone's wrongdoings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Disappointing' looks like it describes the scene, but it gives its own word, with the rearranged scene following it.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words name wrongful acts or breaches of law.

clue.text: Price is often changed for first book illustration

indicators.note: changed tells you the letters of the words price is often are rearranged

explanation.surface: A remark that the cost of something frequently alters.
explanation.walkthrough: 'changed' rearranges the twelve letters of PRICE IS OFTEN.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the picture facing a book's title page, the first illustration a reader meets.

clue.text: Response from the chorus?

indicators.note: from signals that the letters are taken out of the run of words the chorus

explanation.surface: A choir replies to a soloist.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a sung reply; 'from' points to letters straddling the two words that follow.
explanation.definitionFit: A reflected sound comes back like a reply, so it can be called a response.

clue.text: Select choc-ice not cold at the centre

indicators.note: not says a piece is to be removed from the ice-cream bar
at the centre fixes where the removal happens, in the middle of the word

parts.note: a choc-ice is a chocolate-coated ice-cream bar
C is the standard abbreviation for cold, as on taps

explanation.surface: Someone picks a chocolate ice-cream that isn't chilled in the middle.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove the middle C (cold) from CHOCICE; 'Select' is an adjective meaning high-quality, not a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe something of fine quality, picked out as the best.

clue.text: Scope of betting in this place?

parts.note: SP is the starting price in horse-race betting
here means in this place

explanation.surface: Someone asks what the range of gambling is at this venue.
explanation.walkthrough: SP, short for starting price, is the odds at the moment a race begins in British bookmaking.
explanation.definitionFit: A field or range of influence, as in a sphere of activity, is its scope.

clue.text: Energetic person needs Monday off

indicators.note: off suggests the word Monday is disordered, its letters set wrong

explanation.surface: A busy person needs a day off from work at the start of the week.
explanation.walkthrough: 'off' looks like time off, but it signals rearranging MONDAY.
explanation.definitionFit: A tireless go-getter is likened to an electrical generator.

clue.text: Bear twins but make little of it?

indicators.note: twins asks for two copies of the bear's name, one beside the other

parts.note: Pooh is A. A. Milne's Winnie-the-Pooh

explanation.surface: Two bear cubs that are twins, although someone dismisses it.
explanation.definitionFit: To dismiss scornfully is to belittle, treating something as trivial.

clue.text: Lucid accounts of windows set high in church-walls

parts.note: lucid means clear
accounts are tales or stories

explanation.surface: Clear narratives about the high windows of a church.
explanation.definitionFit: A clerestory is the upper row of windows in a church nave; this is an old spelling, plural.

clue.text: Close-fisted on the cards

explanation.surface: Someone tight with money appears in a card reading.
explanation.definitionFit: Near is an old word for stingy, and something near is approaching or likely soon.

clue.text: Tone-lowering characters in apartments

explanation.surface: People who drag down a neighbourhood live in the apartment blocks.
explanation.definitionFit: In music, the sign that lowers a note by a semitone is a symbol on the stave; British homes on one floor are apartments.

clue.text: Mark left by breaking head off film award?

indicators.note: breaking head off says the award loses its first letter

parts.note: the Oscar is the Academy Award for films

explanation.surface: A statuette shows a mark where its head snapped off.
explanation.definitionFit: A blemish remaining on the skin after a wound heals.

clue.text: First capital gains tax in Berkshire

parts.note: A is the first capital letter of the alphabet
scot is an old word for a tax, as in scot-free

explanation.surface: An early capital gains tax is levied in an English county.
explanation.walkthrough: 'capital gains tax' looks like one phrase, but splits as A, link 'gains', and SCOT. Ascot, in Berkshire, England, is famous for its racecourse.
explanation.definitionFit: The racecourse town lies in that English county west of London.

clue.text: Feeling of resentment from the summit, we hear

indicators.note: we hear tells you the word for summit is only spoken, giving a word with the same sound

parts.note: the peak is the summit of a mountain

explanation.surface: Someone feels bitter on the mountain top.
explanation.definitionFit: Pique is irritation from wounded pride, a form of resentment.

clue.text: Potter's work in amassing hemp pieces, strangely

indicators.note: pieces, strangely tells you the letters of amassing hemp are broken up and oddly rearranged

explanation.surface: A potter gathering bits of hemp for a craft project.
explanation.walkthrough: The Potter is not a ceramicist but Stephen Potter, who wrote the 1947 book on winning games by dubious ploys.
explanation.definitionFit: Stephen Potter's humorous book title names the art of winning by psychological tricks.

clue.text: Many revs make small cars go!

parts.note: Minis are small British cars
a go is an attempt or try

explanation.surface: Lots of engine revolutions make little cars run.
explanation.walkthrough: 'revs' looks like engine speed but means reverends: clergy taken together.
explanation.definitionFit: The clergy as a body, many reverends, form the church's ministry.

clue.text: Peach popular now and in the past!

parts.note: in means fashionable at the moment
former means of earlier times

explanation.surface: A peach that is fashionable today and was so before.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Peach' is slang for informing on someone, so the definition is a person who does that.
explanation.definitionFit: To peach is old slang for betraying accomplices, so a peacher is a snitch.

clue.text: Physique and health organisation

explanation.surface: A health body caring for people's physical shape.
explanation.definitionFit: A person's bodily makeup and vigour is their constitution, and the makeup or structure of a body is too.

clue.text: He left Anglo-Saxon rebel for the bounty

indicators.note: left says the word He departs from the rebel's name

parts.note: Hereward the Wake led English resistance to the Normans
taken as written

explanation.surface: A fugitive outlaw leaves the Saxon rebel for the price on his head.
explanation.walkthrough: Hereward the Wake resisted William the Conqueror in the fens of East Anglia.
explanation.definitionFit: A bounty is a sum paid for a service, such as capturing an outlaw.

clue.text: Not much of a painting but an important item

explanation.surface: A small piece of a painting turns out to matter.
explanation.definitionFit: A close-up of a small part of a picture is a detail; it also means a single particular or point.

clue.text: Always right after a vigil?

indicators.note: after places the letter for right behind the word for vigil

parts.note: an eve is the evening or day before a festival, a vigil

explanation.surface: Someone is permanently correct after keeping watch through the night.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words mean at all times, without end.

clue.text: Brush handle?

explanation.surface: A question about the grip of a paintbrush.
explanation.definitionFit: To brush is to make light contact, and to handle is to feel with the hands.

clue.text: Look! I would go into bathing-pool!

indicators.note: go into places the contraction for I would inside the word for look

parts.note: lo is an old word meaning look
I'd is short for I would

explanation.surface: An excited swimmer announces they are heading into the outdoor pool.
explanation.definitionFit: A lido is a public open-air swimming pool.

clue.text: Fish daily

explanation.surface: A fish eaten every day.
explanation.definitionFit: Char is a trout-like fish; a daily is British slang for a cleaning lady, also a charwoman.

clue.text: Game for Kitty

explanation.surface: A game played with a cat.
explanation.definitionFit: Pool is a cue game like billiards, and also the shared fund of stakes in betting.

clue.text: One frightened Miss Muffet off, and chair was broken

indicators.note: was broken says the letters of and chair are smashed and reassembled

explanation.surface: Little Miss Muffet was scared away and her seat broke.
explanation.walkthrough: In the nursery rhyme a spider sat down beside Miss Muffet and frightened her away.
explanation.definitionFit: The rhyme's spider belongs to the eight-legged class of creatures.

clue.text: Weaver's bed?

parts.note: the weaver is Shakespeare's Nick in A Midsummer Night's Dream, and a bed is also the base of a river or sea

explanation.surface: A question about where a weaver sleeps.
explanation.definitionFit: The character's surname also means the lowest part, like a riverbed.

clue.text: Duke takes sherry, sadly, in bars

parts.note: oloroso is a dark sweet sherry

explanation.surface: A nobleman drinks sherry miserably in pubs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bars' looks like pubs but means bars of music, where the direction tells players to sound sorrowful.
explanation.definitionFit: It is an Italian musical direction for playing mournfully.

clue.text: Performer for each receiving present

indicators.note: receiving means the word for each takes another word into its middle

parts.note: per means for each
to lay is to present, as in lay a case before a court

explanation.surface: An entertainer gets a gift for every show.
explanation.definitionFit: An actor or musician on stage is a performer.
